blocks.heading: Exfoliation
blocks.text: Exfoliation is the detachment of outer rock sheets or layers, often giving an exposed surface a rounded or peeling appearance. Thermal stresses can contribute where surface heating and cooling create differences in expansion and contraction between outer material and the interior. Repeated stresses may help fractures grow and sheets separate. The account concerns changes in the rock’s stress and shape, rather than chemical conversion of the whole block into a new mineral. Repeated peeling rounds the outcrop into an exfoliation dome, and the fallen sheets and fragments collect as scree at its foot.

A thermal-exfoliation sequence can show an exposed outer layer warming and expanding, subsequent cooling and contraction, then the growth of surface-parallel cracks and eventual sheet detachment. The diagram should keep the core and outer layer distinct. It should not place ice within a joint unless the intended mechanism is freeze-thaw. The simplified sequence describes a contributing mechanism, not a claim that daily temperature change alone explains every exfoliation surface. Unloading and other stress changes can also contribute in particular landscapes.

blocks.text: USGS research on a monitored granite dome provides evidence that thermal cycling and cumulative surface heating can contribute to exfoliation-related cracking. This supports attention to the mechanism without turning it into a universal single-cause explanation. In a resource task, describe the supplied heating, cooling and peeling evidence and avoid inventing a temperature or rock composition. The process connects weathering to rockfall hazards and to later erosion of loosened material. A rounded outcrop may record a long history of physical and chemical processes; its present shape alone cannot reveal a complete chronological sequence or a precise rate of change.
